info.title: Streamlit agent API
info.summary: Drive a running Streamlit app without a browser.

servers.description: Relative to this document's URL. Resolve it against the URL you fetched this document from, which gives a URL ending in `/`, then append each path without its leading `/`. Resolving the paths against the origin instead would skip any prefix a proxy strips, such as a hosting platform's, and reach the platform rather than the app.

post.summary: Send client state, run the app, read the result.
post.description:
One request is one client-state transition: send what you want changed, the app runs, and you get the finished result. Omit `session_id` to create a session; `{}` is the simplest request. The request blocks until the run chain settles, including reruns from callbacks, `st.rerun()`, or a page redirect.

A request with no changes reruns the app. It re-applies nothing, so a trigger never fires twice, but code that runs on every rerun runs again. You rarely need one, since a session does not change on its own between interactions. Send one to close a dialog, refresh a `run_every` fragment, or pick up data that changed outside the app.

**A timeout is not a failure.** A run that outlasts `server.agentWaitTimeout`, such as a first load of uncached data, returns `202` with `wait_timed_out` and the `session_id`, and keeps going. Send only `session_id` to wait for it instead of starting it over. The same request again also collects it, except after a creating call, where the same request, having no `session_id`, creates another session. Any other request gets `session_busy` while that run is still going; once it has finished, another request runs instead, and the timed-out run's result is not returned. After a request that failed without any response, also send only `session_id`, and check the result before sending your changes again.

Reuse one session: each creating call runs the app from the start and holds a session until it has been idle for `server.agentSessionTTL`. There is nothing to close.

A session runs as whoever created it. Where the deployment maps identity headers into `st.user` (`server.trustedUserHeaders`), the app sees the caller's user, and only that identity can use the session. Otherwise it is anonymous, and an app behind `st.login` shows its signed-out state; calling `st.login()` does not sign this session in. The app reads each request's headers as `st.context.headers`, minus `Cookie`, `Authorization`, and `Proxy-Authorization`.

create.summary: Start a session and read the app

submit_form.summary: Fill a form and submit it

parameterized_report.summary: Open a page with bound query parameters, in one call

200.description: The run chain settled; `status` says whether the app raised.

202.description: Not a failure: the run is still going. An `Error` with code `wait_timed_out` and the `session_id`; send only `session_id` to collect the run.

default.description: A refused request. An app that raised is not one: that is a 200 with `status: "error"`.

200.description: The OpenAPI document for this API.

post.summary: The same protocol as a remote MCP server.

schema.description: One JSON-RPC 2.0 request, notification, or response. A batch is refused with a `200` response.

200.description: A request's JSON-RPC response: its result, or an error such as `-32601` for a method this server does not implement. A refused tool call is a result. A batch gets one `-32600` error here too.

202.description: A notification or a response, accepted.

400.description: Refused with a JSON-RPC error: `-32700` for a body that is not JSON, and `-32600` for one that is not a JSON-RPC message, for a web page's request without `Content-Type: application/json` (`invalid_request`), for an unsupported `MCP-Protocol-Version`, and for `server/discover`, which this server does not implement, so a client falls back to `initialize`.

session_id.description: An opaque handle from a previous response. Omit it to create a session. An unknown or expired handle is an error, never a silent fresh start.

widget_state.description:
Element keys from the latest `actions` mapped to JSON values, shaped like `st.session_state`. Unmentioned elements keep their values. Not allowed on a creating call, since keys exist only once the app has run.

Refused with `invalid_value`:
- The wrong JSON type for the element's `value_schema`. A number is text only where it names an option, and text is never a number; `1.0` counts as `1` where the schema says `integer`. Dates and times are ISO 8601 text, a slider's included: `st.datetime_input` and `st.time_input` take any ISO 8601 layout and refuse other text, and an offset the widget's values lack is refused. A single-value element reads a one-item list as its item and refuses any other list, `[]` included, and a list over `maxItems` is refused. `null` inside a list is refused.
- A value outside `options`, or over `max_selections`.
- A label several options share, unless the widget accepts new options.
- A value the widget cannot read.

Otherwise a value is applied as the app applies it, so read `value` in the response: an out-of-range number, a malformed `st.date_input` date or color, or a short slider range resets to the default; a fraction sent to an integer `st.number_input` or slider is truncated; text past `max_chars` is cut; and a reversed slider range is kept, so send the lower value first. A value between `step` increments is not refused. `null` resets a widget to its default, unless its node has `clearable: true`: a browser user can empty it, and `null` does. `[]` clears a list. Checks only a browser runs, `required` and `validate`, are not applied.

One request is one rerun, so a widget it removes, such as a field of a mode it switches away from, is gone afterwards. A widget whose generated key the request changes, such as a slider whose bounds another value moved, drops the value sent for it without an error. Check each key you set is still there with that value. A form's fields go with one of its submit triggers; with `clear_on_submit`, send every field each time, since fields keep their values here. Keys in an open `st.dialog` go on their own. Controls outside an open dialog stay usable. Any full rerun, including a request with no changes, closes the dialog unless the app opens it again. When its `on_dismiss` is `rerun`, the dialog's own key fires its dismiss; with `ignore` it has no key.

trigger.description: At most one trigger to fire. Omit the field to fire nothing; `{}` is malformed.

page.description: The `url_path` of a page in `pages`, never a Python path. Defaults to the app's default page on creation, the current page otherwise. An unknown one is refused with `unknown_page` before anything runs, except on a creating call: there the app first runs its default page, and the error carries the `session_id` to continue with.

query_params.description: Replaces the URL parameters; omit it to keep them. A parameter bound to a widget (`bind="query-params"`) sets that widget, so one creating call can open a parameterized report. One equal to its widget's default is ignored, so move a widget back with `widget_state`, and one its widget cannot take is dropped with a `200`, leaving the widget as it was. A bound widget keeps its value when its parameter is left out, so `{}` clears only unbound parameters. At most 1000 values and 524288 characters once encoded.

timezone.description: An exact IANA name, such as `Europe/Berlin`.

locale.description: A BCP 47 language tag, such as `de-DE`.

context.description: What a browser reports about itself, read by the app as `st.context.timezone` and `st.context.locale`, both `None` when unset, and `st.context.timezone_offset`, derived from the timezone. Held for the session: omit it to keep the last one, send a new one to replace it, and `{}` clears both. It never changes how values are encoded.

InteractRequest.description: Navigation (`page`, `query_params`) is a separate transition and cannot be combined with widget changes. `null` in any field but `session_id` is the same as omitting it.

key.description: The key of an element whose `actions` entry has kind `trigger`.

value.description: Text or selected option supplied by the widget.

Trigger.description: A trigger resets after the run that saw it.

schema_version.description: Fields are added within a version: tolerate unknown fields and element types.

session_id.description: Pass this back to continue the session.

status.description:
- `ready`: the run chain settled, the run was not marked failed, and the page shows no uncaught exception.
- `error`: the app raised, so the tree stops at the raise and `actions` may shrink; act on this snapshot. The session stays usable. It is also reported while an exception from an earlier full run is still on the page, such as after a fragment rerun. A script that failed to compile leaves only the error in `main`, and no `actions` until it compiles.

observed_at.description: When this snapshot was assembled, for citing an answer. After a fragment rerun, content outside the fragment is as an earlier run left it, as in a browser. A fragment with `run_every` does not refresh on its own here: its content is as the last request that reran it left it.

pages.description: Every page of the app. A single-page app has one, named after its script.

query_params.description: The URL parameters as the app has them: URL state, not a record of what produced a number, which the widgets' `value`s are. Setting a bound widget drops its parameter until the app writes it back. A page change keeps only embed parameters and bound ones whose widget is on the new page.

tree.description: The current page as a tree: the root containers `main`, `sidebar`, `event` (dialogs and toasts), and `bottom`, with every container's children in order. Collapsed content rendered eagerly is included; content that never ran is not.

actions.description: Everything you may do now, each with its element's `type` and `label`. Before sending a value, read the element with the same `key` in `tree`: its `value_schema` and `props` say what to send. An element that is disabled, has a `support` reason, or is in a closed dialog is in the tree but not here.

undescribed_types.description: Coverage gaps: internal payload names of elements whose command did not describe itself, such as an element replayed from an `st.cache_data` entry a browser session filled. Such a node is named after its payload, which can match a command's name, so this list is what marks it. Normally absent.

Node.description:
One element or container in the app's tree.

`type` is the public Streamlit command that emitted it, such as `selectbox` or `line_chart`, and each `props` key is one of that command's parameter names, spelled as a user writes it (`label`, not `title`), apart from a few facts Streamlit derived, such as a media element's `url` or an exception's `message`. The Streamlit API reference at https://docs.streamlit.io/develop/api-reference documents them, so this document does not.

`props` is how the element was built, `value` what a widget holds now, `value_schema` what a request sends it, and `data` what Streamlit derived, such as a table's preview. Presentation, such as width or alignment, and content the author never supplied are omitted. A media URL in `props`, such as an image's `url`, is relative to the request, like `data.url`; resolve every URL with `urljoin`, which leaves an absolute one, such as a link's, as it is.

Values are plain JSON, here and in table previews: dates and times are ISO 8601 text, decimals are strings, durations are seconds, non-finite numbers are `null`, and binary data is `{"bytes": <length>}`. Table values are as stored, not as displayed: no `format` and no time zone conversion.

type.description: The public Streamlit command name; or one of the root container names `root`, `main`, `sidebar`, `event`, `bottom`; or, for an element listed in `undescribed_types`, its payload name.

key.description:
How to address the element in a request: the author's `key=` when set, stable and readable, and otherwise a generated element ID, an opaque session-scoped handle to read from the latest snapshot, never to construct, parse, or persist. Absent for elements without identity, such as most display commands.

A key is an identity, not an invitation: `actions` lists the keys you may act on, and an element inside a container marked `support` is not addressable. A generated key changes when the widget's parameters do, such as a slider's bounds, so after such a change find the element again by its `label` in `actions`.

props.description: The command's parameters under their public names, with effective values where they change what the element means or how it is used (`disabled`, `expanded`, `options`, bounds), so a flag such as `disabled` is reported even when false; a documented default, such as `unsafe_allow_html=False`, may be left out. A few report state rather than an argument: a dialog's `is_open`, a plain popover's or plain tab's `open`; a stateful `st.tabs`, `st.expander`, or `st.popover` reports that state as its `value`. A widget bound to the URL reports `bind`, and its key names the `query_params` entry that sets it.

value.description: What a widget holds now, in the form a request sends back: a `format_func` widget's formatted label, and typed new text as typed. Sending it back unchanged is valid, except a label several options share. Absent for a display element, whose content is in `props`; for a trigger, whose payload resets once its run finishes; and for a password input, which can be set but is never reported.

value_schema.description: The JSON Schema of what a request sends this element, in its `widget_state` entry or a trigger's `value`, in the form `value` is reported: the type, `format: date` for dates, and a range's item count. Legal values are in `props`. In `widget_state`, `null` is accepted on top; a trigger's `value` must match the schema. What is refused or adjusted is listed under `widget_state`.

clearable.description: `true` when a browser user can empty the widget, such as an `st.selectbox` with `index=None`: `null` then clears it rather than resetting it to its default. Absent otherwise.

data.description: Facts Streamlit derived about the element's data, as opposed to parameters the author wrote.

support.description:
Why the element is not fully usable, absent when it is. A container's reason applies to everything inside it.
- `browser_required`: what renders comes from JavaScript this interface does not run (custom components, `components.html`, inline iframe HTML, `st.html` with `unsafe_allow_javascript=True`); the source or arguments are still reported.
- `action_unsupported`: a browser user can act on the element, and this interface only reports that: data editor edits, uploads and recordings, deferred downloads, and dataframe and chart selections and dataframe button columns where the app enabled them.

Explain such a gap, or fall back to a browser, rather than report incomplete output as complete.

form_id.description: The owning `st.form`. Send its fields with exactly one of its submit triggers; omitted fields keep their values.

fragment.description: The owning `st.fragment`, an opaque id to compare, not parse. An `st.dialog` body is one. Keys all in one fragment rerun only it, leaving the rest of the page as it was; keys across regions rerun the whole app. An open dialog's keys go on their own, apart from keys outside it and keys in a fragment inside it, since a whole-app rerun would close the dialog and discard what was sent to it: such a request is refused with `cross_dialog_batch`. A dialog node carries the fragment of the code that opened it, and its contents the dialog's.

ElementData.description:
An element's data, described rather than inlined.

**Branch on `complete`.** True: what is here is everything, `preview.rows` for a table or `spec` for a chart given a figure. False: `url` serves the rest, or `unavailable` says why it cannot. A preview is never the answer to an aggregate question.

columns.description: Column names and Arrow types, the schema of what `url` serves. A pandas index the data carries is a column, an unnamed one as `__index_level_0__`, even when `hide_index` hides it; a default range index is not. A built-in chart (`st.line_chart`, `st.area_chart`, `st.bar_chart`, `st.scatter_chart`) serves the table its browser plots. Several `y` columns are melted to long form, one row per point: `value -- streamlit-generated` holds y and `color -- streamlit-generated` holds the name of the column a value came from. An unnamed index plotted as x is `index -- streamlit-generated`. Other columns keep the author's names. The chart's `spec` refers to these names.

row_count.description: Absent for a lazily loaded table whose source does not know its size.

complete.description: Whether this block already holds the whole dataset.

preview.description: The first rows. Whether more exist is `complete`.

rows.description: Rows as values in `columns` order, encoded as described on `Node`.

url.description: The complete data as an Arrow IPC stream. Relative to the URL of the request that returned this snapshot, like every media URL in it: resolve it with `urljoin`, not against the origin. Fetch it as often as you need while the element is still rendered. It is a temporary link: once a later run drops the element or the session expires, it can answer `404` at any time, so take it from the latest snapshot and never store or share it.

unavailable.description:
Why incomplete data has no `url`:
- `too_large_to_serve`: over `server.maxMessageSize`; narrow the app's filters.
- `multiple_datasets`: a chart over several dataframes, such as a layered Altair chart; `spec` still describes it.
- `external_url`: the chart's `spec` loads data from a URL, which the browser fetches and this interface does not; fetch it from there if you can.
- `lazy_loading`: a table that loads rows on demand; only the preview is here, and `row_count` is the full table's when its source knows it.
- `undescribed`: an element in `undescribed_types`; only the preview is here.

spec.description: A chart's or map's own specification: the Vega-Lite spec of Altair and the built-in charts, the Plotly figure, the ECharts option, or the Deck.gl spec of `pydeck_chart` and `map`, with a `pydeck_chart` tooltip under `tooltip` as `pdk.Deck` takes it. A figure, option, or Deck.gl spec holds the plotted values itself, with Plotly's base64 typed arrays expanded into numbers, so its block is `complete`. The colors `#000001` through `#000040` in a Plotly figure are placeholders the browser replaces with the app theme's colors and can be ignored. A Deck.gl layer can still name a URL its browser fetches, which is not fetched here. A Vega-Lite chart's table is in `columns`, `preview`, and `url` instead, as is a dataframe given as an ECharts `dataset.source`, which `spec` replaces with a `{"name": ...}` placeholder.

spec_omitted.description: Paths dropped from `spec`, currently the styling in Plotly's `layout.template`. Content a template adds, such as annotations, is kept, and nothing that holds data is dropped.

key.description: The key to use in `widget_state` or `trigger`.

type.description: The element's `type`, as on its node.

label.description: The element's `label`, when it has one, so a generated `$$ID-...` key can be told apart at a glance. Not an identifier: two elements can share one. An element without one, such as `st.feedback` or `st.chat_input`, has no `label`.

url_path.description: The page's public handle, empty for the default page. This is what `page` in a request takes.

help.description: What the page is for, as the author's Markdown from `st.Page(help=...)`. Absent when the page has none. Read it to choose a page without running it.

hidden.description: The page is left out of the navigation menu (`visibility="hidden"`). It still opens by its `url_path`, as its URL does in a browser. Absent when the page is in the menu.

Error.description: A refused request. Usually nothing ran, so the last snapshot you received is still current. The exceptions: `wait_timed_out`, whose run is still going, and an unknown `page` on a creating call, judged after the run, both carry `session_id`; `internal_error` can follow a run; and writes refused after a timed-out run you did not collect were checked against that run's page. After any of these, send only `session_id` to read the page again.

session_id.description: The session to continue with, on `wait_timed_out` and on a creating call that already made a usable session.

code.description:
- `invalid_request` (400): The request is malformed: an unknown field, a field of the wrong type or format, text that is not valid Unicode, `widget_state` or `trigger` on a creating call, navigation combined with widget changes, or a web page's request without `Content-Type: application/json`.
- `request_too_large` (413): The body is larger than `server.maxWidgetStateSize`.
- `invalid_value` (400): A value the element cannot take: of the wrong JSON type, outside its options or over its selection limit, or one the widget cannot read. The message lists the legal options where there are some.
- `not_a_value` (400): The element is a trigger: fire it with `trigger`.
- `not_a_trigger` (400): The element holds a value: set it through `widget_state`.
- `missing_form_submit` (400): Fields of an `st.form` were sent without one of its submit triggers, so they would change nothing.
- `cross_dialog_batch` (400): Widgets in an open `st.dialog` were combined with widgets outside it or in a fragment inside it. Send each region's widgets on their own.
- `cross_form_batch` (400): One request cannot span two forms, or mix a form's fields with other controls.
- `unsupported_element` (400): The element is on the page, but this interface cannot set or fire it: it is display-only, takes input JSON cannot express (uploads), or its `support` field says why.
- `unknown_key` (404): No element with that key exists in this session, or a form, container, or display element with it has left the page. Keys come from the latest snapshot and are never constructed.
- `unknown_session` (404): The `session_id` does not exist or has expired. Omit it to start a new session.
- `unknown_page` (404): No page has that `url_path`. The error's `pages` lists the available ones.
- `not_on_page` (409): The element exists in this session but cannot be used now: it may be on a page you left, appear only after another control changes, be in a closed dialog, or be left from a script that failed to compile.
- `disabled_widget` (409): The element is on the page but disabled; it accepts nothing until the app enables it. Send what enables it in one request, then use it in the next: each request is checked against the snapshot before it.
- `session_busy` (409): The session already has an interaction in flight, or a run whose client timed out or disconnected is still going. Wait for the request in flight; once its client has gone, send only `session_id` to collect the run.
- `wait_timed_out` (202): Not a failure: the run outlasted `server.agentWaitTimeout` and is still going. Send only `session_id` to collect it.
- `internal_error` (500): The interaction could not be completed. The cause is logged server-side and not returned.
- `not_available` (403): The agent API is off. The operator enables it with `server.enableAgentApi`.
- `host_not_allowed` (403): The request's `Host` is not in `server.allowedHosts`.
- `origin_not_allowed` (403): Sent by a web page whose `Origin` is not in `server.corsAllowedOrigins`. Programmatic clients send no `Origin`. Responses carry no CORS headers, so listing an origin only admits callers that CORS does not restrict, such as the app's own page. A page on another origin is stopped at its preflight.
- `too_many_sessions` (429): The server already holds `server.agentMaxSessions` sessions. Reuse a `session_id`, or retry once idle ones expire.

message.description: What went wrong, usually with what to do instead.
